CirclesGeometryTriangles
Game: Move two points on a circle and watch the two straight lines that just touch it; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A and B, or focus one and press the arrow keys. Slide the bar to change the lines and tick the boxes to show the clues.

Drag A or B, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). The slider sets how long AP and BQ are.

Look for the math

Choose two places on a circle, draw the same-length tangent at each, and connect the two points on the circle to the two tangent ends. Bogomolny's page claims that one line always cuts the other exactly in half. Try to break it by dragging the points.

The claim, stated exactly

At A and B on the circle, equal tangents AP and BQ are drawn. Let S be where AB meets PQ. The page says that S is the midpoint of PQ, so PS = QS — in other words, AB bisects PQ. The live cut-the-knot page still embeds the original Java applet, but browsers no longer run Java plug-ins; this page rebuilds the same figure in SVG. The logic test checked the claim over a 48 × 48 grid of circle positions and 41 slider lengths, plus 6,000 random pictures: 102,670 drawable figures, with the largest difference between PS and QS below 1e-10. The claim holds; no correction was needed.

Why the crossing lands in the middle

Put the circle's centre at the origin and write A and B as r(cos a, sin a) and r(cos b, sin b). The applet's tangent at A points a quarter turn from the radius: u_A = (−sin a, cos a), and likewise u_B = (−sin b, cos b). With tangent length ℓ, P = A + ℓ u_A and Q = B + ℓ u_B. Using vectors, the midpoint of PQ is

(P + Q)/2 = (A + B)/2 + (ℓ/2)(u_A + u_B)

The first term is the midpoint of AB, which is on the line AB. For the second, write m = (a + b)/2: then u_A + u_B = 2 cos((a − b)/2)(−sin m, cos m) and B − A = 2r sin((b − a)/2)(−sin m, cos m). They point along the same line, whatever ℓ is. So the midpoint of PQ lies on AB, and the crossing S is that midpoint. Equal lengths matter: with unequal tangents the extra term would not be parallel to AB.

The hint's matching triangles

Extend AP through A to R with AR = AP, and let T be where the two tangents meet. Tangents from one outside point are equal, so TA = TB; adding the equal pieces gives TR = TQ. Triangles ABT and RQT are isosceles and share the angle at T, so they are similar and QR ∥ AB. In triangle PQR, A is the midpoint of PR and AS is parallel to QR, so AS is a midline and S must be the midpoint of PQ. Tick Show hint to see those steps in the picture.

One harmless quirk of the applet is kept: its Compute() stops drawing when the slider reads strictly between −2 and 2, or when A and B are less than two pixels apart, so the last figure stays on screen. An unused helper named Other(), left over from a sibling applet, is not ported: this applet calls Tangent() directly for both points.

Tick Show hint and slide the length through zero: the figure pauses in the middle, but on both sides S stays halfway along PQ.
